The company has described the ADMT's purpose in its Pre-use Notice in general terms — something like "to improve our services," without saying what the ADMT actually decides. The CPPA's regulations require more specific language than that (11 CCR § 7220(c)(1)). In its Final Statement of Reasons, the CPPA explained why: vague language about a planned ADMT use "undermines consumers' exercise of their rights to opt-out of and access ADMT" — a person cannot meaningfully decide whether to opt out of something the notice never actually describes. Whether this company's stated purpose clears that bar is a judgment about this company's own words, not a fixed word count or template. Section 3 addresses whether the notice's purpose statement meets this standard. (California Privacy Protection Agency, Final Statement of Reasons, CCPA Updates, Cyber, Risk, ADMT, and Insurance Regulations, 11 CCR § 7220(c)(1).)
